items.html:
Chilean road lines are either all white, or all yellow:

  • All white road lines are most common. Within the Americas, they are a good clue for Chile, though not completely unique.
  • All yellow road lines are seen in National Parks or areas of high snowfall. Within the Americas, these all yellow road lines are essentially unique to Chile.

You will almost never see a combination of the two colours, apart from a few rare exceptions.

NOTE: It is important to note that Argentina has a decent amount of roads with all white road lines.

Chile has a solid white Google Car with no antenna in Generation 3. There are two variants:

  • A plain white car (left).
  • A white car with a visible black section (right). This car is unique to Chile.

A blue Google Car can be seen in Generation 4.

NOTE: In Generation 3, a plain white Google Car with no antenna can also be seen in Peru and Bolivia.

Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides. They are somewhat similar to Brazilian poles, however have fewer horizontal supports in the indent. The upper part typically has small pinholes.

Wooden poles are also fairly common.

Regular vehicles have white licence plates, while commercial and taxi vehicles have orange plates.

NOTE: Orange plates can also be seen in Ecuador. Brazilian commercial plates are red, but can look similar in some lighting.
Slots can often be seen at the top of signposts.

Chile uses chevrons with a yellow base and black arrows.

NOTE: Argentina uses white with red arrows.
Chilean bollards are similar to Spanish style bollards, with a white reflector at the front and a yellow-orange reflector at the back. They are not super common.
While regular bollards are somewhat rare in Chile, you may sometimes find this orange, temporary bollard, with two white stripes at the top.
Bridges in Chile often have red painted fence posts.

Shown here is a Köppen climate map of Chile.

Chile is a long and narrow country that spans more than 4,000 kilometres from north to south, meaning that its climate varies significantly due to latitude.

The northern parts of the country, which lie in the tropical zone, are dry and arid, leading to a mild desert climate. In the centre, around the capital, the climate becomes less arid, leading to a temperate mediterranean climate. In the southernmost regions of Chile, which lie in the subantarctic zone, the climate is cold and wet, leading to a cool oceanic climate.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._
Chile uses a memorable regional road naming system, where the first letter increases between A and Y from north to south. For more information on specific regions, see here.

Chilean phone codes will sometimes have a two digit area code in front, followed by seven digits. The patterns of the codes are easily memorable. Most of the central states also have different area codes for specific provinces, which can help you make accurate guesses.

The Atacama is an extremely arid desert covering the northern third of Chile. Some parts of it experience the lowest rainfall on the planet. As a result, many locations in this desert are almost completely devoid of any vegetation: you will often just see sand and bare rock without any plants in sight anywhere.

NOTE: The Atacama Desert also covers parts of southern Peru, western Bolivia and northwestern Argentina.

The region of Arica y Parinacota can be recognized by the smooth, sandy mountains that may look slightly eroded, or have bulbous formations. Valleys are also common, which are rarely seen in other parts of Chile.
These rocky, uneven mountains are most commonly seen in Atacama and northern Coquimbo.

This brownish red soil can sometimes be seen in Atacama region.

NOTE: This is most reliable in Generation 3. This soil can be seen in other regions in Generation 4.
Eucalyptus plantations combined with a somewhat dry climate are a good indicator that you are in southwestern Valparaíso.
The region around Santiago can be recognized by its semi-arid climate, having dry hills and scattered vegetation.
Compared to the area around Santiago, the Maule region has a similar look. However, it has a Mediterranean climate, and is generally greener. Vineyards are also commonly seen in this region.

Concepcion pines, scientifically named Pinus radiata, can be recognized by their puffy needles. They are most commonly found in Bio Bio, where the city of Concepcion is located, and less commonly in Ñuble and Araucania.
Narrow roads with trees on both sides can commonly be seen in the regions of Bio Bio and Araucania.

Monkey puzzles, scientifically named Araucaria araucana, are found in far eastern Araucania.

NOTE: Monkey puzzles can also be found on the other side of the Argentinian border.

A rolling, agricultural landscape, comparable to New Zealand, can be seen on Isla Grande de Chiloé.

NOTE: Similar looking landscapes exist in some other parts of the country, but usually more level.
Chilean rhubarb can commonly be found on Isla Grande, and on the mainland east of it. Chilean rhubarb can be recognized by its large, cabbage-like appearance.
Lush green valleys, with rocky mountains and often overcast coverage, can be seen in southern Los Lagos and northern Aysén.
Southern Aysén can be recognised by autumn coverage, having orange and red coloured vegetation. Keep in mind that not all coverage in this region will have fall colours.
Roadlines with dotted paint are common in Los Ríos and Aysén.
The A-31 can be recognised by its high altitude, with a steep drop into a valley to the north. The road also has Gen 3 sunset coverage.

Generation 4 sunset coverage can be seen on Ruta 21 from Calama to San Francisco de Chiu Chiu. In the west near Calama, the sun has just started to set, causing a giant white dome in the sky. In the east, the sky has a warm gradient, and the tops of the volcanoes are seen glowing pink.

More Generation 4 Sunset coverage can be seen on B-710 and Ruta 5.

On the B-710, a slight ridge can be seen to the west, while Ruta 5 is more open. Make sure to use the road angle or other clues before guessing.

Ruta 1 is a coastal road that is easily recognized by the wall of mountains to the east, and the Pacific Ocean to the west. This image shows the various weather conditions faced on the road to help you make closer guesses.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._
Part of Ruta 41 is located in a valley, with snowy mountains seen in the distance. Many trees and vineyards can commonly be seen toward the west. Triple yellow lines can also be seen from this point.
These purple flowers, named Large-leaved Lupines, can commonly be found along Ruta 240.

All yellow lines on a concrete road are a good indicator that you are on a paved road in the Magallanes region, in the very south of Chile. The landscape tends to be barren, grassy, and treeless.

NOTE: Ruta 9 only appears in Generation 3, whereas the other roads only appear in Generation 4 coverage.

A distinct landscape consisting of a line of snow-capped mountains with two other isolated, symmetrical snow-capped volcanoes are seen in Lauca National Park. Most of the roads are newly paved and have a smooth, dark look.
The northern section of Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve can be recognized by the Tamarugo trees lining the road. The road itself is mediocre quality, and in a consistent north-west direction.
Alto Loa National Reserve can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to snow-capped volcanoes. The road running through the reserve is paved.
Smooth mountains with a reddish tint are seen in Los Flamencos National Reserve. Salt pans are also a common sight. The reserve uses triple yellow lines, with short dashes in the west.

In the west, Nevado Tres Cruces National Park can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to a line of mountains. The sand has a reddish tint.

In the east, the Google Car drives up a mountain pass with views of lightly snow-capped volcanoes and snow on the side of the road. The roads in the National Park are paved.

Llanos de Challe National Park can be recognized by the brown coloured dirt on the roadside, patches of light sand, juniper plants, and dark coloured mountains. The sky is overcast in most of the coverage.

NOTE: Pan de Azúcar National Park looks similar, however has less vegetation.

A vast, mostly treeless landscape combined with triple yellow lines are seen in Alto Bio Bio National Reserve. While the reserve may look dry, there is a distinct cold and high altitude feel. Monkey puzzles are also seen toward the east.

NOTE: Ruta 181 leading up to the reserve also has triple yellow lines, however, is less vast with more vegetation.

Puyehue National Park can be recognized by the dense vegetation surrounding the road. The pavement itself has triple yellow lines, and tar snakes are frequently seen. In the east, many dead trees can be seen with a lack of leaves.
A slight, sandy ridge with a gradual incline can be seen in Arica.
A larger, towering ridge can be seen in Iquique.
A rockier, and more uneven ridge can be seen in Antofagasta.
San Pedro de Atacama can be recognized by its clay brick walls, commonly with triangles at the top.
Orange street signs can be seen at almost every intersection in the city of Lanco, and occasionally in the nearby town of Malalhue.

Villa O’Higgins can be recognized by the large mountains located immediately to the east. To the west, snow-capped mountains are seen in the distance. Street signs, fences and many other structures throughout the village are made of orange-stained wood.

Orange lamps can most often be seen in Calama and Chañaral, and rarely in Antofagasta.

NOTE: Orange lamps can rarely be found in other smaller cities. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.
Lamps that look like green domes can be seen in Copiapo.
Lamps in Santiago very commonly have photocells. You will rarely find them in other cities such as Valparaiso, Osorno and Loncoche.
Grey lamps with a thin, flat top and a rounded underside can be found in Talca.
Blue rectangular lamps with a yellow stripe can be found in Concepción.
This lamp, with a silver top and grey bottom, can be found in Puerto Montt and Temuco.
Poles in Arica feature white paint with a black number, while the other cities in the Atacama Desert feature poles with yellow paint. Keep in mind the paint may have faded, making it look white.
Round poles with black paint can be seen in the town of El Salvador.
The Google car can be seen towing a white and silver trailer with the word ‘Outback’ south of the Chilean National Zoo in Santiago.
A grey Toyota Hilux, with various gear loaded and a snorkel on the front right, can be seen from around Baños Morales to this point, where the trekker continues the journey on foot.
Conguillio National Park can be recognized by this white truck with visible side mirrors and an antenna on the front right.

Puerto Williams, the southernmost town covered by street view, can be recognized by this white pickup truck with visible side mirrors.

NOTE: The Puerto Williams coverage is located fairly far away from the normal car coverage in Chile. The nearest normal car coverage is in Fuerte Bulnes, near Punta Arenas.
Note: there are many trekkers in Chile. This section highlights a small selection of some of the most notable and unique ones.
The Atacama Large Millimetre Array can be recognized by the many radio telescopes in a barren, snowy environment.
ALMA OSF can be recognized by the large radio telescopes and rural facilities.

This horse trekker can be seen to the northeast of San Felipe.

NOTE: A similar trekker can be found on the other side of the border in Argentina.
The Torres del Paine area can be recognized by the sharp peaked mountains, and the trekker walking on a glacier along with other people in orange helmets.

lm.note: The A-31 can be recognised by its high altitude, with a steep drop into a valley to the north. The road also has Gen 3 sunset coverage.

lm.name: Landscape - A11 - Barren
lm.note:
After crossing the Lluta River at Poconchile, the Ruta 11 continues out of the valley and up into the mountains. The road is all newly paved (except for a few small segments with ongoing construction) and is generally quite wide. This section of Ruta 11 features:

  • Many concrete barriers (which are often painted yellow), double guardrails, and roadside drainage ways.
  • Maroon-colored asphalt in some places.
  • Mountains are made of light reddish sand with occasional exposed rock. Rounded protrusions are also common

The landscape is bare of vegetation until around Zapahuira, east of which the landscape becomes open and covered with small green bushes.

lm.name: Landscape - A11 - Lluta River Valley
lm.note: Along the Lluta River, the Ruta 11 passes through a wide valley lined by sloping, sandy mountains that often feature distinctly round rock protrusions. The valley is home to a large amount of agriculture relative to other parts of the Atacama Desert. You’ll often see sizable green fields lined by bushes, trees, or wooden fences, as well as bunches of planted Mexican fan palms. A railroad track also follows the Lluta River on both sides, so if you’re in a green valley next to both a river and a railroad, you’re almost certainly on Ruta 11.

lm.note: After crossing the Lluta River at Poconchile, the Ruta 11 continues out of the valley and up into the mountains. lm.name: Landscape - Lauca National Park
lm.note:
East of Putre, Ruta 11 enters Lauca National Park which has a flatter landscape, with tall snow-capped mountains in the background, and features unique Andean Plateau vegetation like Peruvian feather grass and the recognizable cushion plant yareta (Azorella compacta). You can also find Chilean bollards lining the road, which are extremely rare.

Lauca can look very similar to other areas in the east Andes of northern Chile, but it’s recognizable for the iconic Volcán Parinacota, a tall snow-capped volcano that stands alone and away from other mountain ridges. It’s visible from basically every location in the park, though it can be shrouded by clouds.

lm.name: Southern Aysen - autumn coverage
lm.note: Southern Aysén can be recognised by autumn coverage, having orange and red coloured vegetation. Keep in mind that not all coverage in this region will have fall colours.

lm.name: Southern Los Lagos and northern Aysén. - Lush green valleys
lm.note: Lush green valleys, with rocky mountains and often overcast coverage, can be seen in southern Los Lagos and northern Aysén.

lm.name: Southern Valparaiso - Eucalyptus plantations
lm.note: Eucalyptus plantations combined with a somewhat dry climate are a good indicator that you are in southwestern Valparaíso.

lm.name: Alto Bio Bio National Reserve
lm.note:
A vast, mostly treeless landscape combined with triple yellow lines are seen in Alto Bio Bio National Reserve. While the reserve may look dry, there is a distinct cold and high altitude feel. Monkey puzzles are also seen toward the east.

NOTE: Ruta 181 leading up to the reserve also has triple yellow lines, however, is less vast with more vegetation.

lm.name: Alto Loa National Reserve
lm.note: Alto Loa National Reserve can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to snow-capped volcanoes. The reserve does not have any paved roads.

lm.name: Arica Sandy Mountains
lm.note: The province of Arica y Parinacota can be recognized by the smooth, sandy mountains that may look slightly eroded, or have bulbous formations. Valleys are also common, which are rarely seen in other parts of Chile.

lm.name: Atacama Mountains
lm.note: These rocky, uneven mountains are most commonly seen in Atacama and northern Coquimbo.

lm.name: Aysen Autumn
lm.note: Southern Aysén can be recognised by autumn coverage, having orange and red coloured vegetation. Keep in mind that not all coverage in this region will have fall colours.

lm.name: Isla Grande de Chiloe
lm.note:
A rolling, agricultural landscape, comparable to New Zealand, can be seen on Isla Grande de Chiloé.

NOTE: Similar looking landscapes exist in some other parts of the country, but usually more level.

lm.name: Lauca National Park
lm.note: A distinct landscape consisting of a line of snow-capped mountains with two other isolated, symmetrical snow-capped volcanoes are seen in Lauca National Park. Most of the roads are newly paved and have a smooth, dark look.

lm.name: Llanos des Challe National Park
lm.note:
Llanos de Challe National Park can be recognized by the brown coloured dirt on the roadside, patches of light sand, juniper plants, and dark coloured mountains. The sky is overcast in most of the coverage.

NOTE: Pan de Azúcar National Park looks similar, however has less vegetation.

lm.name: Los Flamencos National Reserve
lm.note: Smooth mountains with a reddish tint are seen in Los Flamencos National Reserve. Salt pans are also a common sight. The reserve uses triple yellow lines, with short dashes in the west.

lm.name: Lush Mountain Valleys
lm.note: Lush green valleys, with rocky mountains and often overcast coverage, can be seen in southern Los Lagos and northern Aysén.

lm.name: Maule
lm.note: Compared to the area around Santiago, the Maule province has a similar look. However, it has a Mediterranean climate, and is generally greener. Vineyards are also commonly seen in this region.

lm.name: Nevado des Cruzes National Park
lm.note: In the west, Nevado Tres Cruces National Park can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to a line of mountains. The sand has a reddish tint. In the east, the Google Car drives up a mountain pass with views of lightly snow-capped volcanoes and snow on the side of the road. The roads in the National Park are paved in newer coverage.

lm.name: Puyehue National Park
lm.note: Puyehue National Park can be recognized by the dense vegetation surrounding the road. The pavement itself has triple yellow lines, and tar snakes are frequently seen. In the east, many dead trees can be seen with a lack of leaves.

lm.name: Santiago Landscape
lm.note: The region around Santiago can be recognized by its semi-arid climate, having dry hills and scattered vegetation.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Ruta 21
lm.note: Generation 4 sunset coverage can be seen on Ruta 21 from Calama to San Francisco de Chiu Chiu. In the west near Calama, the sun has just started to set, causing a giant white dome in the sky. In the east, the sky has a warm gradient, and the tops of the volcanoes are seen glowing pink.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: All yellow lines
lm.note: Within the Americas, all-yellow road lines are essentially unique to Chile. These lines are typically seen in National Parks or areas of high snowfall, as Chile usually uses all-white lines.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Empty slot under sign
lm.note: Chile signs commonly have those empty slots at the top of signposts.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Pole
lm.note: Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides. They are somewhat similar to Brazilian poles, however have fewer horizontal supports in the indent. The upper part typically has small pinholes.

lm.name: Arica/Iquique stick
lm.note: In Arica and Iquique, in the very North of Chile, sometimes there'll be a little stick with a few leaves stuck on the car's back.

lm.name: Full White & Yellow
lm.note: • Chilean road lines are either all white, or all yellow.

lm.name: Chile
lm.note: Chilean phone codes will sometimes have a two digit area code in front, followed by seven digits. The patterns of the codes are easily memorable. Most of the central states also have different area codes for specific provinces, which can help you make accurate guesses.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Alto Bio Bio National Reserve - Monkey Puzzle Trees
lm.note: A vast, mostly treeless landscape combined with triple yellow lines are seen in Alto Bio Bio National Reserve. While the reserve may look dry, there is a distinct cold and high altitude feel. Monkey puzzles are also seen toward the east.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Alto Loa National Reserve
lm.note: Alto Loa National Reserve can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to snow-capped volcanoes. The reserve does not have any paved roads.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Conguillo National Park
lm.note: Conguillio National Park can be recognized by this white truck with visible side mirrors and an antenna on the front right.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Lauca National Park
lm.note: A distinct landscape consisting of a line of snow-capped mountains with two other isolated, symmetrical snow-capped volcanoes are seen in Lauca National Park. Most of the roads are newly paved and have a smooth, dark look.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Llanos de Challe National Park
lm.note: Llanos de Challe National Park can be recognized by the brown coloured dirt on the roadside, patches of light sand, juniper plants, and dark coloured mountains. The sky is overcast in most of the coverage.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Los FLamencos National Reserve - Short Dashes
lm.note: Smooth mountains with a reddish tint are seen in Los Flamencos National Reserve. Salt pans are also a common sight. The reserve uses triple yellow lines, with short dashes in the west.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Nevado Tres Cruces National Park
lm.note:
In the west, Nevado Tres Cruces National Park can be recognized by the vast, open landscape, followed by salt pans leading up to a line of mountains. The sand has a reddish tint.

In the east of this park, the Google Car drives up a mountain pass with views of lightly snow-capped volcanoes and snow on the side of the road. The roads in the National Park are paved.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Pampa del Tamarugal National Park
lm.note: The northern section of Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve can be recognized by the Tamarugo trees lining the road. The road itself is mediocre quality, and in a consistent north-west direction.

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Pan de Azucar National Park
lm.note: Pan de Azucar National Park can be recognized by the brown coloured dirt on the roadside, patches of light sand, little vegetation, and dark coloured mountains. The sky is overcast in most of the coverage

lm.map: National Parks of Chile (Major Bajor Learnable)
lm.name: Puyehue National Park
lm.note: Puyehue National Park can be recognized by the dense vegetation surrounding the road. The pavement itself has triple yellow lines, and tar snakes are frequently seen. In the east, many dead trees can be seen with a lack of leaves.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Chilean road lines are either all white or all yellow.
  • You will almost never see a combination of the two colours, apart from a few rare exceptions.

--- NOTE:

  • It is important to note that Argentina has a decent amount of roads with all white road lines.

lm.name: A-31 Lush Mountains
lm.note:
The eastern part of highway A-31 travels high into the Andes through lush green mountains and valleys.

  • Entirely gen 4 and very sunny.
  • Very high elevation, mountains up in the clouds and views of a vast landscape below.
  • Valleys covered in shrubs, bright green grass, and occasional eucalyptus trees.
  • Scattered rocks beside the road and human-made rock walls.

lm.name: Alto Biobío National Park
lm.note: Alto Biobío National Park in Araucania can be recognized by all yellow road lines on a high elevation road usually looking down over a vast mountainous landscape. Monkey puzzle trees, short bushes, and bunches of Chilean bamboo cover the ground.

lm.name: Alto Loa National Reserve
lm.note: Alto Loa can be recognized by its remote and almost completely barren desert landscape featuring reddish gravelly soil and tall snow-capped mountains all around. Salt pans are also common. All coverage is gen 3 and on dirt roads.

lm.name: Bay of Concepción
lm.note: Locations along the Bay of Concepción can be recognized by the presence of water to the east, north, or west, with the other side of the bay usually visible. Coverage is all gen 4 in developed coastal towns with many small beaches and a lot of boating activity. You'll also see lush coastal vegetation and pine forests.

lm.name: Bay of Concepción - Ruta 164
lm.note: The stretch of Ruta 164 that follows the coast of the Bay of Concepción can be recognized by the presence of coast to the north and both sides of the Bay visible to the east and west. It's surrounded by a flat landscape of green coastal vegetation.The highrises of Concepción city are often visible to the south.

lm.name: Beach Road B-440
lm.note: A coastal desert road in gen 3, the B-440 runs along the peninsula north of Antofagasta and is unique in having coast to the south or east. The road is entirely paved and features bright white sandy soil and a long stretch of flatness to the north.

lm.name: Cerro Castillo National Park
lm.note:
Cerro Castillo National Park in Aysén has sunny gen 3 coverage recognizable by its yellow center lines with white outer lines.

  • Landscape is grassy and lightly forested.
  • Tall beige colored snow-capped mountains and jagged rock formations.

lm.name: Chaitén Area
lm.note:
Chaitén is a small remote town in southern Los Lagos, recognizable for the forested mountain range towering over the town and the presence of ash and rubble due to a volcanic eruption.

  • A west coast with a gravelly beach.
  • A river and large dead forest to the east of town.

lm.name: Chiloé Island
lm.note:
Chiloé island is very recognizable due to its lush green rolling landscape, southern vegetation, and unique architecture. Coverage is mostly gen 4 summer, with some areas still gen 3.

  • Rolling green landscape, mild hills and no big mountains. Agricultural and livestock grazing fields surrounded by wooden fences are common.
  • Dense forests of arrayan trees (which have reddish bark), coihue, and eucalyptus.
  • Large hard ferns, iconic Chilean rhubarb, and yellow gorse are common.
  • Unique all-wood architecture with facades of wood shingles. Stilt houses are common.

lm.name: Coastal Road B-430
lm.note:
The B-430 northwest of Antofagasta is a coastal desert road still in generation 3 featuring:

  • Water to the west, reddish sandy soil, and a towering mountain ridge to the east.
  • Often very hazy/foggy coverage.

lm.name: Concepción City Proper
lm.note: Concepción is one of the most populous cities in Chile and thus has sprawling neighborhoods and many highrises, modern buildings, and parks in its downtown area. The city also has a very unique blue and yellow street lamp design. Coverage in Concepción is almost entirely gen 4.

lm.name: Coquimbo City Landmarks
lm.note: The Coquimbo/La Serena urban area is recognizable for being a large coastal city surrounded by a desert-ish landscape. Much of Coquimbo is built on a large hill and features landmarks visible from quite far away: the Third Millennium Cross (a giant metal cross) and the Cultural Mohamed VI (a tall and colorful mosque).

lm.name: East on Ruta 60
lm.note:
East of Rio Branco in Valparaíso, Ruta 60 is recognizable for its gen 4 coverage on a concrete road with all yellow road lines surrounded by dry rocky mountains.

  • Bushes and trees further west near Rio Branco, and low vegetation or bare ground max east.
  • Lots of traffic on the road. Yellow lines on a concrete road is a rare combination, so it's a very good identifier for Ruta 60.

lm.name: Eastern Santiago Northern Roads
lm.note: The mountain road east of Lo Barnechea has all yellow road lines with a single center line. It goes through dry, rocky mountains with dark brown soil. The elevation increases and vegetation decreases as the road goes east. Bare snow-capped peaks can be seen from the easternmost part.

lm.name: Eastern Santiago Southern Roads
lm.note: The main mountain road east of Puente Alto is gen 4 and always has large dry mountains on all sides. The northern part of the road has white lines and goes through small towns; the southern part has all yellow lines, less vegetation, and features tall snow-capped peaks visible in the distance.

lm.name: Embalse el Yeso Gen 3
lm.note: In the mountains east of Santiago, Embalse el Yeso can be recognized by gen 3 coverage traveling along the coast of a bright turquoise reservoir surrounded by extremely tall mountains made of dark rock.

lm.name: Embalse el Yeso Gen 4
lm.note: The mountain road up to Embalse el Yeso is covered in gen 4 on an unmarked road (or a dirt road). It can be recognized by the deep brown rocky soil beside the road and the giant mountains made of dark rock visible all around. Snow is often visible on top of the mountain ridges.

lm.name: Futaleufú National Reserve
lm.note: Futaleufú National Reserve is made up of a dense southern forest in a wide mountain-lined valley recognizable for its high number of Patagonian cypress (with thick trunks and round leaf clusters) and the wooden fencing lining every road.

lm.name: Gen 3 Tamarugo Forests
lm.note:
Tamarugo trees, recognizable for their dark bark and thin, spindly light green leaves, are unique to the central desert plains of Tarapacá.

Smaller clusters of tamarugo trees surrounded by rural houses, signs, and fenced-off land can be found on the A-665 and in the town of La Tirana.

lm.name: Hualpén Peninsula Gen 3
lm.note: The gen 3 coverage on Hualpén Peninsula can be recognized as a mostly flat coastal area featuring subtropical vegetation and unusually deep red soil. You'll always have water to the south and west, with the highrises of Concepción often visible in the distance.

lm.name: Hualpén Peninsula Gen 4
lm.note: Gen 4 coverage on the Hualpén Peninsula can be recognized by a combination of coastal vegetation, grassy fields with dark soil, and lush green forests including planted eucalyptus trees. Coast can often be seen to the north, or to the west where the large port of Talcahuano is visible.

lm.name: La Serena Beach Road
lm.note: The main road going toward Coquimbo along the coastline of La Serena features rows of fancy resorts, planted palm trees, and a great view of Coquimbo peninsula, which is basically one big hill covered in buildings that juts northward into the ocean. The giant metal Third Millenium Cross is often visible.

lm.name: La Serena Historic Center
lm.note: A lot of Spanish neocolonial architecture, very often painted red and white, is a defining feature of La Serena's Historic Center. "La Serena pavement," made of red tiles and with black or grey tiled patterns, is found on most sidewalks (and some roads) in the historic center.

lm.name: Laguna del Laja National Park
lm.note:
The eastern part of road Q-45 goes into Laguna del Laja National Park, which features a vast landscape and recognizable lush snow-capped mountain ranges.

  • Coverage is all gen 4 on an unpaved road with dark grey or brown dirt.
  • Western part is green and forested. Yellow flowers are common.
  • The middle part features a blue sparkling lake with snow-capped mountains all around.
  • The eastern part by the Argentina border has an open landscape and low greenish vegetation.

lm.name: Lake Jeinimeni National Reserve
lm.note:
The south part of the X-753 goes into Lake Jeinimeni National Reserve, recognizable for its gen 3 overcast coverage in a fall-colored southern beech forest located right next to snow-capped mountains.

  • Parts of the reserve have snow on the ground.
  • Trees have greyish-brown bark and deep orange or red leaves.
  • Lake Jeinimeni itself has clear blue water and is lined by snow-capped mountains.

lm.name: Lauca National Park
lm.note:
Generation 3 coverage on a paved road through a barren desert landscape with snow-capped mountain ridges to the north and west is typical of Lauca National Park.

  • The snow-covered Parinacota Volcano is the most distinctive feature of the park.
  • Soil is rocky and covered with small bushes and the green cushion plant "yareta".

lm.name: Llanos de Challe National Park
lm.note: Foggy and overcast gen 4 coverage on a paved desert road along the coast is characteristic of Llanos de Challe. The surrounding soil is an orange-brown color, somewhat rocky, and covered in small dark green bushes. There will always be coast west and a large mountain ridge to the east, though the coast can appear quite far away.

lm.name: Los Flamencos National Reserve
lm.note:
Los Flamencos National Reserve has gen 3 or gen 4 coverage on a paved road, all yellow roadlines, and a barren desert landscape.

  • Gravelly soil that is red or pink. Many hills that look like large sand dunes.
  • Snow-capped mountains can be seen in the west, flatness and random rocks can be seen in the east.

lm.name: N-31 Mountain Pass
lm.note:
The eastern part of the N-31 is all gen 4 on an unpaved gravel road going through a wide mountain pass. It features:

  • Very dark and rocky soil. Lots of random rocks beside the road.
  • Dense forest all around, with many bare leafless trees. Small ferns and moss cover the forest floor.
  • Significant snow cover on surrounding mountains.
  • The Ñuble River is often visible close to the road.

lm.name: N-55 East of Recinto (Gen 4)
lm.note:
From Recinto to Las Trancas, the N-55 is a gen 4 road with winter coverage in a forested mountain valley.

  • All yellow road lines, wooden fences and stone gutters along the road.
  • Temperate forest in winter, featuring many bare trees. A lot of bright green Chilean bamboo next to the road.
  • Closer to Las Trancas, lots of snow on the ground and on mountain slopes.

lm.name: N-55 Gen 3
lm.note: The far eastern part of the N-55 has distinct gen 3 winter coverage on a dirt road going up a mountain slope. The road is surrounded by a trees that are often bare and leafless. A large snow-covered mountain ridge is visible close to the east. Near the top of the mountain, there's snow beside the road.

lm.name: Nevados Tres Cruces National Park
lm.note:
In Nevado Tres Cruces National Park, Ruta 31 is gen 4 on a wide road with all yellow road lines and dark, grainy asphalt.

  • A semi-open landscape with snow visible on the surrounding mountains.
  • Red-and-yellow snow poles with a rectangular yellow tag on top.
  • Further east, there's dark volcanic soil and a lot more snow on the ground.
  • Max east, Laguna Verde has bright blue water and dark mountains in the background.

lm.name: Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve
lm.note: Tamarugo trees, recognizable for their dark bark and thin, spindly light green leaves, are unique to the central desert plains of Tarapacá. Gen 4 coverage through a tamarugo forest usually indicates Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve where the flat, barren desert suddenly transitions into a large forest.

lm.name: Patagonia National Park
lm.note: Gen 3 sunny summer coverage on a thin dirt road in a green mountain valley characterizes Patagonia National Park in Aysén. It is a lush rolling grassland with large hills south and a massive, snow-capped mountain range to the north. A particular green cushion plant ("Patagonian Azorella") is endemic to the area.

lm.name: Puyehue Max East
lm.note: The far eastern part of Puyehue National Park features all yellow road lines on a poor-quality road with tar between the center lines. Recognizable white-and-yellow snow poles line the road. The surrounding landscape is a high-altitude coihue forest with light sandy soil.

lm.name: Puyehue National Park
lm.note: In gen 4, all yellow road lines on a poor quality road (with cracks, potholes, etc.), surrounded by a southern beech forest with dense undergrowth is characteristic of Puyehue National Park. The undergrowth features a lot of ferns, bamboo, and Chilean rhubarb. In the eastern part of the park, all of the trees look dead and are completely bare of leaves.

lm.name: Q-45 East of Antuco
lm.note:
East of Antuco, the Q-45 runs through a very recognizable green mountain valley. It features:

  • Gen 4 coverage on a nicely-paved road with all yellow road lines. Some sections are overcast while others are bright and sunny.
  • Tall mountain ridges on both sides, covered in dense green forest.
  • Many mountains go up through the clouds, and some mountains are snow-capped.
  • In sunny coverage, blooming yellow flowers are everywhere.

lm.name: Road R-95-S
lm.note:
Road R-95-S is covered in gen 4 on a light gravel road running through a vast and open landscape surrounded by mountains.

  • Small shrubs and round tufts of grass cover the hills.
  • Sparse forests of pines and southern beech trees cover the landscape.
  • A large number of Monkey puzzle trees can also be seen.

lm.name: Road W-887
lm.note:
The W-887 in max south Los Lagos is short but very memorable. It can be recognized by overcast or rainy coverage on a dark dirt road surrounded by Patagonian trees.

  • It often has white sand/ash on or alongside the road.
  • Lots of Chilean rhubarb and massive hard ferns.
  • Sometimes there are visible water droplets on the camera.

lm.name: Road X-753
lm.note:
The X-753 goes south of Chile Chico and is recognizable by entirely overcast gen 3 fall coverage, a dark brown dirt road, and a very dry mountainous landscape.

  • Reddish soil covered in small yellow or green bushes. Basically no trees or human activity at all.
  • A distinctive snow-covered mountain range to the west.

lm.name: Ruta 11 in the Mountains
lm.note: Up in the mountains, Ruta 11 features gen 4 on a newly-paved road with a reddish tinge, surrounded by a high altitude landscape composed of completely bare pinkish mountains and bright white rocks. Double guardrails, concrete barriers (sometimes painted yellow), and active construction sites are all common.

lm.name: Ruta 11 in the Mountains (with vegetation)
lm.note: Up in the mountains and around Zapahuira, Ruta 11 features all gen 4 coverage on a wide, newly-paved road with a high altitude mountainous landscape that is covered in small green or grey bushes. The surrounding mountains are typically rounded on top, with snow-capped peaks sometimes distantly visible to the north.

lm.name: Ruta 11 River Valley
lm.note:
Ruta 11 is entirely sunny gen 4 coverage. The river valley section is recognizable for:

  • Sloping, sandy mountains on either side of the valley.
  • Large agricultural fields and planted Mexican fan palms.
  • A railroad runs along the entire valley and is often visible north or south of the road.

lm.name: Ruta 115
lm.note:
In eastern Maule, Ruta 115 travels deep into the Andes through a beautiful mountain valley. Coverage is all early spring gen 4 and has yellow road lines (either yellow center or all yellow).

  • The valley is extremely wide and has temperate forest vegetation. Many trees are bare due to the season.
  • Immense rocky mountains covered in trees, grass, and shrubs are always visible. Many have snow-covered peaks.
  • The easternmost stretch goes to high altitude and has scarce vegetation and a lot of snow everywhere.

lm.name: Ruta 15 Eastern Part
lm.note:
Far east on Ruta 15 is gen 4 on a paved road surrounded by a semi-flat landscape covered in Peruvian feathergrass and small shrubs, with towering mountains in the distance.

  • Soil is light, reddish, and very sandy.
  • Andean plateau vegetation like feathergrass, tola, and yareta are common.
  • Mountain ranges are often snow-capped and they appear closer further east.

lm.name: Ruta 15 in the Andean Plateau
lm.note:
The eastern part of Ruta 15 is a gen 4 paved road that goes through the high altitude Andean Plateau. It has:

  • Light brown or reddish soil that is covered in feathergrass, the spindly tola shrub, and occasionally the green blob-shaped yareta. rolling hills
  • Round rolling hills with occasional exposed cliff faces.
  • One section around Chapire has all yellow road lines.

lm.name: Ruta 15 Max East Grassland
lm.note:
Right near the Bolivian border, Ruta 15 goes through a flat green grassland surrounded by towering, often snow-capped volcanoes.

  • Coverage is all gen 4. Ruta 15 itself is paved, side roads are unpaved.
  • Buildings often use Bolivian-style red brick architecture.
  • Small waterways and grazing llamas are also common.

lm.name: Ruta 181
lm.note:
Ruta 181 in Araucania can be recognized by sunny gen 4 coverage on a road with all yellow roadlines. It particularly features:

  • A vast open landscape surrounded by large rocky mountains.
  • Lush green forests on mountainsides.
  • Open grassy fields between hills, often enclosed by wooden fences.
  • An abundance of planted poplar and mediterranean cypress trees.

lm.name: Ruta 225 in Los Lagos
lm.note:
Ruta 225 in Los Lagos runs between Puerto Varas and Petrohue and is recognizable for its unique infrastructure, beautiful views, and native coihue forests. It features:

  • Completely gen 4 coverage, unique wooden guardrails, and a paved two-way bike lane next to the road.
  • Dark soil and a lot of ferns growing from the ground.
  • Dense forest of coihue, particularly further east.
  • Views of the snow-capped Osorno and Calbuco volcanoes.

lm.name: Ruta 240 and Río Simpson
lm.note:
Ruta 240 to Puerto Aysén is recognizable for being summer coverage on a concrete road with a single yellow center line.

  • It goes through a wide valley between huge mountains that have exposed cliff faces.
  • Area is very forested with southern beech trees and planted poplars.
  • Purple flowers (large-leaved lupines) and Chilean rhubarb along the road.

lm.name: Ruta 31, West of Nevado Tres Cruces
lm.note:
Sunny gen 4 coverage on an unmarked desert road with red or dark brown soil strongly indicates Ruta 31. Notably, the section west of Nevado Tres Cruces National Park features:

  • Usually very red soil and a complete lack of vegetation, especially on unpaved sections. Paved sections have no road lines.
  • Large, sloped mountains with rounded peaks. Visible snow on some mountains.
  • Large Y-shaped metal pylons running alongside the road.
  • Part of the road climbs to high altitude and has significant snow on the ground as well as yellow-and-white snow poles.

lm.name: Ruta 41 Gen 4
lm.note:
In Coquimbo, where Ruta 41 enters the Andes, it has distinct gen 4 coverage on a paved road that features steep snow-capped mountains visible to the east.

  • Large rocky mountains on all sides; lots of snow cover atop the tallest mountains.
  • All yellow road lines start around Miraflores and continue further east.
  • Planted trees and fenced-off vineyards closer to Vicuña. Many vineyards go right up to the base of mountains.

lm.name: Ruta 9
lm.note:
Ruta 9 in Magallanes is a unique concrete road with yellow center and outside lines surrounded by a Patagonian landscape.

  • It's gen 3 and usually has overcast coverage.
  • Flat or slight rolling hills covered in grassy fields and sparse trees.
  • Part of it runs along an eastern coast.
  • Close to Cerro Castillo there are much more significant hills.

lm.name: Ruta 9 Divided Section
lm.note:
Ruta 9 in Magallanes is a concrete road with yellow road lines, surrounded by a Patagonian landscape of dark soil and grassy hills.

  • Starting at the Punta Arenas airport and going south through Punta Arenas, Ruta 9 is a divided highway.
  • Punta Arenas is a large and recognizable urban area and is usually visible.

lm.name: Ruta 9 Max South
lm.note:
Ruta 9 in Magallanes is iconic and very distinct. It's unique for being a concrete road with yellow center and outside lines, combined with a deep south Patagonian environment of dark soil and rolling grassy hills.

  • Max south, starting around Bahía Carrera, it turns into an unpaved grey dirt road and enters a southern beech forest.
  • Check the distance and angle of the eastern coast to make precise guesses.

lm.name: Rutas 201/203
lm.note:
Rutas 201 and 203 in Los Ríos have gen 4 coverage, all yellow road lines, a forested mountainous landscape, and views of large blue lakes.

  • Forests have a dense understory of hard ferns, moss, and Chilean bamboo.
  • Early spring coverage, so many trees have sparse light green leaves.
  • Many views of Lake Calafquén or Lake Panguipulli, with pure blue water and large snow-capped mountains in the background.

lm.name: Rutas 21 and 25 Sunset Coverage
lm.note: The stretch of highway on Ruta 25 to Calama and on Ruta 21 from Calama to San Francisco de Chiu Chiu has memorable gen 4 sunset coverage, recognizable by how dark it is and its generally east-west road angle.

lm.name: San Pedro de Atacama
lm.note:
The town of San Pedro de Atacama is a sizeable settlement (by Atacama desert standards) recognizable for the abundance of iconic adobe (mudbrick) buildings.

  • The adobe used is a reddish/deep brown color but is often painted white and red.
  • Adobe walls frequently have unique triangular ornamentations.
  • The large Licanabur volcano is often visible to the north/east.

lm.name: Santa Catalina Tamarugo Forest
lm.note:
Tamarugo trees, recognizable by their dark bark and thin/spindly green or yellow leaves, are unique to the central plains of Tarapacá. A stretch of Ruta 5 near Santa Catalina passes through a Tamarugo forest.

  • It's all sunny gen 4 and looks similar to Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve.
  • A line of scissor-topped poles run to the east along this stretch of road.

lm.name: The "Devil's Throat"
lm.note:
Just north of San Pedro de Atacama, there's scenic gen 4 coverage in a shallow canyon so-called the "Devil's Throat". It has:

  • Reddish, rocky canyon walls displaying sediment layers.
  • Unique sharp and wavy rock formations.
  • Greyish-green shrubs and tufts of grass.

lm.name: V-69 Near Cochamó
lm.note:
The V-69 in southeastern Los Lagos runs along a beautiful fjord with water west and views of huge snow-capped mountains across the water.

  • All coverage is gen 4 on a road that's paved north of Cochamó and unpaved south of it.
  • Recognizable snowy mountains with visible clouds hovering below the mountain peaks.
  • The town of Cochamó is recognizable as a cluster of houses on the coast of the fjord and surrounded by massive snowy mountains.

lm.name: Villa O'Higgins
lm.note:
Villa O'Higgins, the southernmost town in Aysén, is recognizable by gen 3 sunset coverage in a small, organized town surrounded by massive snow-capped mountains.

  • Coverage was taken late fall, so the southern beech forests around the town display deep orange leaves.
  • Soil is dark brown or grey.
  • Houses are made entirely of wood with sheet metal roofs.
  • Streets are usually made of small alternating stone tiles and have stone curbs on either side.

lm.name: Villarrica National Park
lm.note:
Ruta 199 through Villarrica National Park can be recognized by sunny gen 4 coverage on a wide paved road, all yellow road lines, and a landscape of towering mountains and dense forests.

  • Mountains often feature exposed cliff faces.
  • Often has concrete drainage ditches on both sides of the road.
  • In the southeastern part, you'll often see Monkey puzzle trees and the enormous Lanín volcano.

lm.name: Viña del Mar Coastline
lm.note:
Viña del Mar/Valparaíso is Chile's largest coastal city, most recognizable by its fancy highrises, hilly neighborhoods, and beautiful coastline. The road going along its coast is covered in gen 4 and features:

  • Water close to the west and tall city highrises close to the east.
  • An avenue of fancy white hotels and resorts along the coast; many planted palm trees along the road.

lm.name: X-25 Max East Sunset Coverage
lm.note:
The max east part of X-25 in Aysén features dark sunset coverage, fall colors, a mostly flat barren landscape, and low-lying mountains in the background.

  • Coverage is on a dark grey dirt road.
  • Surrounded by small bushes and round tufts of grass; landscape almost completely devoid of trees.

lm.name: X-25 Sunset Coverage
lm.note:
East of Seccion Tapera in Aysén, the X-25 is very recognizable for its late sunset coverage, striking fall colors, and semi-dry landscape with sparse trees and low bushes.

  • Sunset coverage gets later the further east you go.
  • Coverage is on a dark grey dirt road.
  • Hills around the road; a large snow-capped mountain ridge off to the north.

lm.name: Y-150 and Y-156 in Torres del Paine
lm.note:
Going through Torres del Paine National Park in Magallanes, the Y-150 is recognizable for its rocky mountainous landscape, dark soil, and dry Patagonian vegetation.

  • A dark (almost black) northwesterly snow-capped mountain ridge close to the road.
  • "Iceland-esque" grassy hills with areas of dark exposed rock.
  • Runs along multiple bodies of water.

lm.name: Y-290 in Torres del Paine
lm.note:
Going into Torres del Paine National Park in Magallanes, the Y-290 is recognizable for gen 3 sunset coverage in a mountainous landscape covered in dark soil and dry Patagonian vegetation.

  • Sparse forests of short southern beech trees all around.
  • A dark northwesterly snow-capped mountain ridge.
  • "Iceland-esque" grassy hills with areas of dark exposed rock.
  • Runs along multiple bodies of water.

lm.name: pole
lm.note:
Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides. They are somewhat similar to Brazilian poles, however have fewer horizontal supports in the indent. The upper part typically has small pinholes.

Wooden poles are also fairly common.

top.html:
Chilean road lines are either all white, or all yellow:

  • All white road lines are most common. Within the Americas, they are a good clue for Chile, though not completely unique.
  • All yellow road lines are seen in National Parks or areas of high snowfall. Within the Americas, these all yellow road lines are essentially unique to Chile.

You will almost never see a combination of the two colours, apart from a few rare exceptions.

NOTE: It is important to note that Argentina has a decent amount of roads with all white road lines.
top.raw: Chilean road lines are either **all white**, or **all yellow**: - All white road lines are most common. Within the Americas, they are a good clue for Chile, though not completely unique. - All yellow road lines are seen in National Parks or areas of high snowfall. Within the Americas, these all yellow road lines are essentially unique to Chile. You will almost **never** see a combination of the two colours, apart from a few rare exceptions. NOTE: It is important to note that Argentina has a decent amount of roads with all white road lines.

top.html:
Chile has a solid white Google Car with no antenna in Generation 3. There are two variants:

  • A plain white car (left).
  • A white car with a visible black section (right). This car is unique to Chile.

A blue Google Car can be seen in Generation 4.

NOTE: In Generation 3, a plain white Google Car with no antenna can also be seen in Peru and Bolivia.

top.html:
Regular vehicles have white licence plates, while commercial and taxi vehicles have orange plates.

NOTE: Orange plates can also be seen in Ecuador. Brazilian commercial plates are red, but can look similar in some lighting.

top.html: Slots can often be seen at the top of signposts.
top.raw: **Slots** can often be seen at the top of signposts.

top.html:
Chile uses chevrons with a yellow base and black arrows.

NOTE: Argentina uses white with red arrows.
top.raw: Chile uses chevrons with a **yellow base **and **black arrows**. NOTE: Argentina uses white with red arrows.

top.html: Chilean bollards are similar to Spanish style bollards, with a white reflector at the front and a yellow-orange reflector at the back. They are not super common.
top.raw: Chilean bollards are similar to **Spanish style** bollards, with a white reflector at the front and a yellow-orange reflector at the back. They are not super common.

top.html: While regular bollards are somewhat rare in Chile, you may sometimes find this orange, temporary bollard, with two white stripes at the top.
top.raw: While regular bollards are somewhat rare in Chile, you may sometimes find this **orange**, temporary bollard, with **two white stripes** at the top.

top.html: Bridges in Chile often have red painted fence posts.
top.raw: Bridges in Chile often have **red painted** fence posts.
